utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Madam Registrar. Could you kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. For the record all the accused are here, and I think we are full house -- no, I don't see Mr. Bourgon. Okay. And Prosecution is like yesterday, Mr. McCloskey and Ms. Janisiewicz. Thank you. Any preliminaries? None. So let's bring the -- and let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm rising at this point to try and clear up, clarify, and advance what is becoming a growing problem in the case with three of the most important documents, P377, P378, and P379. That's the Zvornik Brigade duty officer's workbook as we now call it for the July period. What we call the war diary, that's P378; and the workbook for the later period running into September, that's P379. We are fast approaching the anniversary of Mr. Thayer's undertaking to have those documents translated. I think I can probably give you the date. It was early December when we were promised by the Prosecution that those documents would be translated, and we still don't have them. There's an illogicality in their exhibit status at the moment. P377 is marked for identification. P378, which is 152 pages in B/C/S but only five of which are translated into English, has been exhibited. And P379, which is completely untranslated I think, is marked for identification. My submission is that P378 should not be exhibited pursuant to your response to Mr. Thayer in December of last year, it should be marked for identification purposes only, but I also invite the Prosecution to give us an update on where we're going with this. A year ago we asked for I think something like 80 pages of those documents to be translated, and upon the Prosecution's undertaking we withdrew those requests for translation because the Prosecution told us they would have the whole document translated. And now we're in prejudiced position, and during the course of my cross-examination I had to bite my tongue not to react to the criticism of me for using untranslated documents, because I was using documents that the Prosecution had undertaken to have translated. And we're getting towards the end of the Prosecution case and these are three of the most important documents in the case and they are still, in relation to two of them, marked for identification; and in relation to the third one should be marked for identification. So I get that off my chest now, and I invite the Prosecution to state now on the record and in open session when we can expect to have those documents translated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I see well, because there is -- yeah, Mr. Thayer is here but I can't see him. Mr. Thayer or Mr. McCloskey, who's going to handle this? I'm assuming that Mr. Thayer is busy preparing for the celebration of the anniversary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You may be getting tired of hearing from me, I'm certainly tired of talking, but we have had the key parts of this translated. There's a few parts that Mr. Haynes is interested in one or two lines in various dates in September and October that we've now put in. We are trying to convince CLSS and our own resources to continue the translation of hundreds of pages that no one can really point to specific relevance to, aside from that they're fascinating documents and they're full of facts and details, and I understand the Defence wants them translated. I will check where we are on that and see. But as you know, this institution, as it's always been, is buried in this kind of work and it's hard for even us to get this done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I take it that the pages that need to be translated have been definitely identified by you and others, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, they haven't, because we had this debate a year ago, as I say. We had 80 pages pending translation. I can probably go back to that list and give them to the Prosecution and say these are the 80 pages we're interested in. But we were stopped in our tracks by the undertaking that the Prosecution would have the whole document translated, and, you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Okay. Thank you, Mr. Haynes. Mr. Thayer. Yes, I can now see you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The last I had checked on that issue, and I think I provided an oral update at the time, was that we were -- and I was told very close to having the entire document completely translated. That's where I thought it was some months ago. I have not followed up since then, nor have I had any requests from anybody as to the progress or with respect to any particular portions of the document. So frankly it hasn't been something that's been brought to my attention as a need from any party. We are checking right now to find out exactly where it is, but my understanding was that the entire document was very close to being translated. We had in fact worked, as I understood it, with Mr. Haynes and his team because there had been other portions translated by CLSS independently of what we were doing from our team, and we, I thought, had integrated those translations so there wouldn't be a duplication of work. We're following it up, but again my understanding was that we were very close to completing the entire translation, and that was some time ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Please, our understanding of this was or has been that there was an ongoing undertaking that it will be concluded without further delay, and my understanding also on Mr. Haynes's position is that he's been raising this matter periodically, voicing his concern that this job had not yet been completed. So tomorrow morning, please, Mr. McCloskey or Mr. Thayer, come back to us with a definitive report on where we stand unless you are in a position to update us even today.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I will do that. We share Mr. Haynes's concern, and so we're together on this, that's not a problem, and I understand frustrations. Though, I do want to update you. We do have a product that we will be providing you based on -- and partially a request of Mr. Bourgon, where we have a -- the English translation on one side and the B/C/S on the other and where the English translation is trying to mirror the B/C/S so that when you see the translation you can actually see where it's coming from. And we've also identified from our handwriting experts and the evidence that's come in who's written down the various parts of this book and so that you will see it. This is done for the key dates from the 12th through about the 23rd. I have asked my colleagues to look into that, to double-check the -- our work, the translations, and offer any other pages they want to have translated. So you can see this in this form, it really makes a difference. I've heard some word back, mostly supportive. So if there's anything else anyone has to they want us to put into this exhibit, let us know and we'll get that together, but it's not meant to replace the big translation for everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That still constitutes good news, and I thank you for that, Mr. McCloskey. Shall we -- are we ready for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe -- and I think we're still in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, no, we are in open session and we have been for the past 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think we should be in closed session from what I gather.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Private session. I don't think we need to move -- whatever the difference. Closed session. Let's go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Today is my last appearance as co-counsel on behalf of Mr. Popovic. I would like to thank the Trial Chamber for the courtesy that you've showed me when I've appeared before you. I would like to thank the court staff for their assistance and generally for the experience that I've had while I've been here and I thank the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Condon. Actually, when I was at home yesterday going through some material, well I decided to check my e-mail again which I do every hour or so and only to come across advance information that this was taking place. And to be honest with you, it came to -- as a surprise to all of us. Usually this is not a common occurrence, but it has happened and that has happened in the past. And when it happened, usually I always took it upon myself to say a few words which I'm going to do as well. We had grown accustomed to your presence here and your intervention, your active intervention in the case, and of course we will miss you, not just us but I think everyone else who has been happy finding himself or herself happy to work with you. I think as time goes by you will be remembered here, you will be remembered for a few things, at least speaking for myself. You will be remembered for the way you can greet the Trial Chamber with a smile even when you are absolutely angry with some of our decisions and you can still put on a smile and that is a very useful asset for any lawyer that looks ahead to a colourful and good career. You will also be remembered for having put us professional Judges in inverted commas which made us muse for quite some time whether we were supposed to be in a niche or whether it was a way of describing it, but anyway we remember that instance with some -- with a smile, with a smile. And we will also remember you because in our hearts we all know that your presence here for over a year, if it has shown anything, it has shown that you have got a great career ahead of you and while you are away pursuing your next stage in your career, we will be remembering you and we will be thinking of you. And we have no doubt in our mind that we will -- not for a moment, that a great road lies ahead and that you will have a great career, Ms. Condon. You will also be remembered for the change in your face when I - and I apologise once more - addressed you as Ms. Cubbon instead of Ms. Condon. These are events that are usually not -- one doesn't cancel them by means of a rubber, they stick in the mind. And brings me to an end. I speak on behalf of my colleagues but also my staff, including John Cubbon. I wish you all the best in your career and I'm sure that our wish will be respected by destiny.

utterances.speaker: MS. CONDON
utterances.text: Thank you for those comments, Your Honour, they're very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think the position being what it is, I think we need to meet tomorrow morning at 9.00 just the same, and then we take it up from there. All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of November, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.49 p.m.,
